source: Vessey (1985) Expertise in debugging computer programs: a process analysis
finding: The founding study. Expertise was DEFINED by chunking ability on the program being debugged, then compared with debugging strategy. Propositions are stated for further testing, not proven.
numbers: 16 programmers from one organisation, verbal protocol analysis. Propositions: experts breadth-first plus system view, smooth flow; novices depth-first, or breadth-first without system thinking, erratic flow.
limits: Circular by design: the expert label comes from chunking, so chunking cannot independently predict strategy. N=16, single firm, single program. Abstract says novices may ALSO be breadth-first but lack a system view, so breadth-first alone is not the marker.
agent_relevance: Treat 'breadth-first plus system view' as an untested hypothesis. Do not hard-code it into the schema as an established expert trait.

source: Glasz et al. (2025) Can LLMs Replace Humans During Code Chunking?
finding: Directly tests LLMs doing the chunking of legacy code that human experts do. LLM-chosen partition points match expert partitions best among automatic methods, and docs written from LLM chunks beat docs from human chunks.
numbers: Legacy MUMPS and IBM assembly (ALC) files; 3 expert partitioners (2 MUMPS, 1 ALC with 40+ years). LLMs GPT-4o, Claude 3 Sonnet, Mixtral, Llama 3. 16 partitioned versions per file; token limits 512/1024/2048/4096; 2,002 module comments; 1.28M GPT-4o grading calls. LLM-partition comments up to 20% more factual (less hallucination) and up to 10% more useful/complete (ALC) than human-partition comments.
limits: Grader is GPT-4o (LLM-as-judge, told to be a hard grader; ICC2k 0.960 MUMPS, 0.908 ALC across 10 repeats). Agreement with experts is lower for ALC (sparse expert split points). Gains vary by model and language; no single best method. LLM-vs-human benefit may reflect chunk size fitting context, not better 'expert' chunks.
agent_relevance: Chunking can be a model slot checked by code: ask the model for split points, check size limits in code, re-query if a chunk is too long (the paper did this). Judge chunk quality by the downstream task, not by match to human experts.

source: Glasz et al. (2025) Can LLMs Replace Humans During Code Chunking? (fixed-length baseline)
finding: Naive fixed-length chunking barely overlaps expert partitions and gave the least factual comments; structure-aware chunking (single module, LLM partitions) did best. Context length correlated positively with quality in MUMPS but not in ALC.
numbers: MUMPS: positive correlation between context length and quality, p=8.80e-10 (as printed); not in ALC. Fixed-length chunks had minimal overlap with expert split points.
limits: Coefficient not extracted; only the p value was read. Different languages gave different best methods, so no one-size-fits-all.
agent_relevance: If our agent must read long code, cut on logical units, not on a fixed window. Test per language.

source: Kou et al. (2024) Do LLMs Pay Similar Attention Like Human Programmers When Generating Code? (FSE)
finding: Six LLMs attend to different parts of the task description than human programmers, whatever the attention method. About a quarter of generation errors trace to five attention patterns.
numbers: 6 LLMs (GPT-4, InCoder-1.3B, CodeGen-2.7B, PolyCoder-2.7B, CodeParrot-1.5B, GPT-J-6B); 12 attention methods in 3 families; 211 incorrect snippets analysed by hand; 27% of errors explained by 5 patterns; user study N=22 (mean 5.62 years programming) favoured perturbation-based (SHAP) attention; 14 of 22 lacked trust in LLM attention.
limits: Attention was over the natural-language task description, not code reading, so it tests keyword salience not code chunking. Human labels were keyword annotations (Cohen kappa 0.64 to 0.73).
agent_relevance: LLMs do not weight task text like humans. Supports not trusting model-reported focus (G2). Does not show LLMs lack chunks.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) EyeMulator: Improving Code Language Models by Mimicking Human Visual Attention
finding: Human gaze priors (what developers fixate, and the order) used to reweight token losses. Positive gains in all 36 model-task-data cells across 6 backbones.
numbers: 6 backbones, 2 data regimes, 3 CodeXGLUE tasks. Relative gains by cell from about +0.2% to +34.4% (best on completion and translation; summarisation METEOR +2.7% to +10.8%). Most frequent fixation bigrams: function declaration to variable declaration 8,399; conditional to loop 6,026. Boilerplate and linear-body gains near 0% (+0.2%, +0.0%); one multi-statement control-flow subcategory +47% to +59%.
quote: even state-of-the-art models continue to distribute attention uniformly across boilerplate and logic
limits: Fine-tuning method, not a prompt. Paper says attention-distribution measures are 'smaller and task-dependent' and used as diagnostics. Small developer pool. Not a test of Vessey's strategy claim.
agent_relevance: Gains come from control flow and dependencies, not boilerplate. A scaffold could mimic this by giving code-computed structure slots (conditions, loops) instead of full text.

source: EyeLayer (2026, ICPC) gaze priors for LLM code summarisation
finding: A learned attention module trained on developer eye tracking improves code summarisation across five models. The claim that the layer learns human-like focus rests on a case study, not a measured alignment score.
numbers: 27 developers, 625 annotated samples, 64 functions. Models LLaMA-3.2-1B/3B, Qwen3-1.7B/4B, CodeBERT. Qwen3-1.7B BLEU-4 13.36 to 15.12 (+1.76 absolute; the 13.17% headline is relative); ROUGE-L 21.39 to 26.67; Llama3.2-1B BLEU-4 14.31 to 16.18; Llama3.2-3B 15.64 to 16.86.
limits: Gains are small in absolute terms (about 1 to 2 BLEU points for most models). No quantitative human-attention alignment result in the part read (last 6k characters of the page not read).
agent_relevance: Weak support only. Do not cite as proof that LLMs now chunk like experts.

source: HumanLLM (2025) Enhancing Code LLM Training with Programmer Attention
finding: Fixation-based reward for CodeT5 raised summarisation a lot but did not help completion or translation. A boundary condition for 'expert attention helps everything'.
numbers: 15 professional developers, 120 Java methods (30 to 50 lines). Summarisation BLEU 5.36 to 10.32, CodeBLEU 8.51 to 15.67, dataflow 18.01 to 32.98. Completion CodeBLEU 5.42 to 4.77 (-0.65). Translation CodeBLEU 15.18 to 14.94. Over 95% of attention shifts occur within three lines.
limits: 10% sample of CodeXGLUE; CodeT5-base only, low baselines (BLEU 5.36); one seed; alpha not specified. Small human sample.
agent_relevance: Human reading is mostly local (95% of shifts within 3 lines). Expert benefit is task-specific; test on our own task before adopting.

source: Le, Nguyen, Nguyen (2026) Do Machines Struggle Where Humans Do? LLM and Human Comprehension of Obfuscated Code
finding: Reasoning-tuned small models rank code difficulty like humans; instruct and coder-tuned models do not. Obfuscation by renaming identifiers (loss of beacons) hurts models.
numbers: 12 models (6 small, 6 medium). Spearman rho with human difficulty: Phi-4 Mini 0.47, DS-R1-Qwen-7B 0.37, SmolLM3-3B 0.36, Qwen3-0.6B 0.30; Llama-3.1-8B 0.08 (p=0.44), CodeLlama-7B 0.02, DS-Coder-6.7B 0.10. Dataset A: 20 snippets x 5 tiers; human study 50 undergraduates. DS-R1-Qwen-7B accuracy 63.8% (L0) to 56.2% (L3); humans 40.46% to 31.09%. Accuracy vs CoT length rho=-0.520 (p=1.1e-4). Adversarial renaming with high semantic displacement: accuracy 21.25%, 10% confident-wrong.
limits: Models are small (0.6B to about 8B). Human group is students; expert humans few (55.56% at one tier). Dataset B size is stated as both 250 and 50 snippets. Block-model level breakdown not reported. Correlations are moderate at best.
agent_relevance: Names act as beacons for models too: misleading names cost accuracy. Long CoT signals a hard item (a free impasse signal for G1, not a schedule).

source: Rong et al. (2026) On Behavioral Alignment of Model-Code and Human-Code Understandability via Behavioral Proxies
finding: LLM understandability judgments align more with professional developers than with students. Role-conditioned prompting did not improve alignment with students.
numbers: Four behavioural proxies P0 (question answering) and P1 to P3 (intent summarisation with semantic self-consistency). Numeric results not in the abstract (only the abstract was read).
limits: Abstract only; sample sizes and correlations not read. Built on a prior human-rated study.
agent_relevance: Role prompts ('be a novice') do not make a model behave like a novice. Do not use persona prompts to simulate skill level (agrees with G4).

source: Wang et al. (2024) How Does Naming Affect LLMs on Code Analysis Tasks?
finding: Replacing variable or method names with nonsense or misleading names degrades CodeBERT on code search and clone detection. Names work as beacons.
numbers: Eight datasets masking variable or function names. Code search MRR fell as low as 17.03 (Java) and 23.73 (Python) in the worst cases as printed in the text read.
limits: The PDF text was garbled in places, so the table-to-cell mapping is uncertain; use only the direction of the effect. CodeBERT is an encoder, not a modern chat LLM; the GPT case study is small.
agent_relevance: Keep readable names in code shown to the agent; strip them only when testing for memorised answers.

source: Wu, Thalmann, Dayan, Akata, Schulz (2025, ICLR) Building, Reusing, and Generalizing Abstract Representations from Concrete Sequences
finding: A chunk-learning model (HVM) that builds chunks then turns recurring slots into variables matches human recall time. LLMs do not transfer the variable the way humans do.
numbers: 112 human participants (variable group vs control, 40 training trials). HVM negative log-likelihood vs human recall time: R=0.86 in training, R=0.7 in transfer (both p<0.001). Associative learner and all LLMs (GPT-2, 3 Llama 2, 2 Llama 3) did not separate transfer from control training. LLMs correlate with human time in training but far less in transfer.
limits: Colour-letter sequences, not code. Likelihood probe of LLMs, not prompting; chat-tuned frontier models not tested.
agent_relevance: Chunk reuse with variables (a function with a hole) is a human skill LLMs show weakly in context. Supports an explicit, code-held library of reusable chunks.

source: Wu, Alaniz, Schulz, Akata (2025) Discovering Chunks in Neural Embeddings for Interpretability
finding: Chunks can be extracted from RNN and LLaMA hidden states; perturbing these states turns related concepts on or off.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only; no code experiments mentioned.
agent_relevance: Shows chunk-like units exist inside models, but nothing says they match programmer chunks.

source: Yu (2025) Adaptive Token Boundaries: Integrating Human Chunking Mechanisms into Multimodal LLMs
finding: Proposes dynamic tokenisation modelled on human chunking for multimodal models.
numbers: +7.8% on Visual QA and +5.3% on complex scene description over unspecified state-of-the-art baselines (abstract).
limits: Single author, abstract only, vision-language, not code. Baselines and sample sizes not read.
agent_relevance: Low weight. Shows 'chunking' is invoked in model design, with no evidence for code.

source: Aytes, Baek, Hwang (2025) Sketch-of-Thought: Efficient LLM Reasoning with Adaptive Cognitive-Inspired Sketching
finding: A prompt scaffold with a 'Chunked Symbolism' paradigm (from working-memory chunking, Miller 1956) and 'Expert Lexicons'. Cuts output tokens a lot at about equal accuracy; a router picks the paradigm.
numbers: 18 datasets in the abstract; average token cut over 74% vs CoT, up to 84%, accuracy typically within 1%. Qwen-2.5-32B 82.30% vs CoT 82.24% at 74.36% fewer tokens; GPT-4o 84.55%, 0.09 below CoT. By type: SVAMP maths Chunked Symbolism 93.70% at 30 tokens; MedQA Chunked Symbolism 73.10% vs Expert Lexicons 85.70%; CommonsenseQA Chunked Symbolism 40.00% vs Conceptual Chaining 84.60%.
limits: Chunked Symbolism fails outside maths (40% on CommonsenseQA), so the router matters. No code tasks. 'Chunking' here means compact symbols, not program chunks.
agent_relevance: Compressed reasoning can keep accuracy. The router result is a warning: choose the reasoning style by task type, in code, not by the model.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) cAST: Enhancing Code RAG with Structural Chunking via Abstract Syntax Tree
finding: Cutting code at syntax boundaries (AST nodes merged under a size cap) beats fixed-size line chunks for retrieval and generation.
numbers: Chunk cap 2000 non-whitespace characters. RepoEval Recall@5: BGE 69.8 vs 67.4, GIST 75.0 vs 70.7, CodeSage 83.9 vs 82.1. RepoEval Pass@1 StarCoder2: GIST 57.9 vs 51.2, CodeSage 73.2 vs 67.6. SWE-bench Lite (300 problems) Pass@1 with Claude-3.7-Sonnet: BGE 16.3 vs 13.7, CodeSage 16.7 vs 14.0, GIST 15.0 vs 14.7. SWE-bench Recall@5 gains only 0.7 to 1.1.
limits: SWE-bench gains are small and one retriever (GIST) is almost flat (+0.3). Single run, no intervals on the page read. Compared only against fixed-size chunks.
agent_relevance: Machine analogue of programmer chunking: meaningful units beat arbitrary windows. Cheap, code-run, fits our rule that code selects.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: Top-down hierarchical localisation (file, then class/function, then edit lines) with no agent loop reached 32.00% on SWE-bench Lite at $0.70 per issue. Skipping the middle level made localisation worse.
numbers: 32.00% = 96 of 300 issues, $0.70. Ablation: 'direct from file-level' edit-location accuracy 47.00% vs 50.67% for the default hierarchical greedy path (row alignment from PDF text; treat as approximate). Authors: the model 'becomes confused' with large context.
limits: Coarse-to-fine is a design choice here, not a test of Vessey's claim. 32% is far below later agent scores. 3.7-point ablation gap on 300 problems, no interval.
agent_relevance: Closest working analogue of an expert 'system view first' strategy in an LLM pipeline: coarse map, then narrow. Worth a cheap test as a state-order rule.

source: Le et al. (2024, ICLR) CodeChain: Modular Code Generation through Chain of Self-revisions with Representative Sub-modules
finding: Asking for modular sub-functions, clustering them and feeding representatives back raises pass@1. But asking for modular code alone (CoT) made direct generation worse.
numbers: Relative pass@1 gain 35% on APPS and 76% on CodeContests. APPS pass@1: GPT-3.5 22.33 to 30.24; WizardCoder-15B 7.90 to 10.50; Competition level GPT-3.5 5.42 to 12.38. CodeChain+GPT-4 61.50% on the Olausson set, above Self-repair+GPT-4 with human feedback.
limits: Without self-revision, CoT for modular code lowered performance vs plain prompting (authors' own finding). Needs public tests to filter before clustering. Comparison sets differ across tables.
agent_relevance: A reusable-chunk library built from verified sub-modules works, but only inside a revision loop with tests. Fits G3.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning Code Generation with Large Language Models
finding: Plan first as short structured steps, then write code step by step: a top-down view before details.
numbers: Pass@1 up to 25.4% relative over direct generation and up to 11.9% over CoT, several benchmarks and languages (abstract). Human raters preferred correctness, readability, robustness.
limits: Abstract only; benchmark count not read. 'Up to' numbers are best cases.
agent_relevance: Plan-then-code is the machine form of breadth-first with a system view. Evidence it helps; no evidence it matches expert human strategy.

source: Li et al. (2023) Structured Chain-of-Thought Prompting for Code Generation
finding: Reasoning in program structures (sequence, branch, loop) beats free-text CoT for code.
numbers: Pass@1 up to 13.79% over CoT on HumanEval, MBPP, MBCPP with ChatGPT and Codex (abstract).
limits: Abstract only; older models; 'up to' best case.
agent_relevance: Structure-shaped intermediate steps (like expert program plans) beat prose steps. Cheap prompt change.

source: Zelikman et al. (2023) Parsel: Algorithmic Reasoning with Language Models by Composing Decompositions
finding: Hierarchical decomposition into function descriptions, with implementations searched against tests. Large gains on hard problems.
numbers: APPS: pass rates over 75% higher than direct AlphaCode and Codex sampling. HumanEval pass@1 67% to 85% with auto tests. Robot plans more than twice as often judged accurate.
limits: Abstract only. Gains depend on tests; auto-generated tests can be wrong (G3).
agent_relevance: Decomposition into named chunks plus code-run tests is the strongest machine evidence that chunk-and-compose helps.

source: Concept-Guided Interpretability via Neural Chunking (2025; seen in a title list, not opened)
finding: Seen in a title list only: treats neural activity as chunks to find concepts.
numbers: none read
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Skip until read.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces (recalled, not opened)
finding: From memory: SWE-agent shows files through a fixed-size window and concise search to keep context small. Chunk size is set by design.
numbers: Figures not verified this session.
limits: Not opened; verify before citing numbers.

source: Adelson (1981, 1984) problem solving and abstract categories in programming (search snippet only)
finding: Search snippet only: experts' recall chunks larger than novices' (about 3.5 vs 2.4 items); experts organise by function, novices by syntax; experts distort recall toward prototypes.
numbers: Chunk size 3.5 vs 2.4 items as reported by a secondary source in search results.
limits: Not opened; secondary summary. Sibling angle agents hold the primary.
agent_relevance: Human baseline for LLM comparison: I found no LLM test of this recall paradigm.

source: McKeithen, Reitman, Rueter, Hirtle (1981) Knowledge organization and skill differences in computer programmers (search snippet only)
finding: Search snippet only: skill differed in recall of normal programs but not of scrambled ones.
numbers: ALGOL W five-phase experiment, details not read.
limits: Not opened; from a search snippet.
agent_relevance: The scrambled-program control is the test no LLM paper found here ran: do models recall real code better than shuffled code? Gap in the literature.

finding: Search snippet only: a CHREST modelling paper said that, against common belief, experts can recall random material better than non-experts.
numbers: none read

source: Johnson and Soloway (1985) PROUST; Rich and Waters (1990) Programmer's Apprentice (recalled, not opened)
finding: From memory: older AI systems that recognise stored programming plans (chunks) in code to diagnose bugs. An early machine use of 'experts hold plan chunks'.
numbers: Numbers not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Pointers only.
agent_relevance: Precedent for a plan library held in code and matched against attempts. Fits our code-held schema.

source: Gap note: no LLM study found replicating Shneiderman recall (real vs scrambled code) or Vessey breadth-first vs depth-first
finding: In about 40 fetches and 2 working searches (web search budget ran out; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API refused), no paper tested LLMs on expert recall of scrambled code, or labelled LLM debugging as breadth- or depth-first.
numbers: Negative search result; not proof of absence.
limits: Coverage limited by tool rate limits. Search may have missed work.
agent_relevance: Treat chunking-as-expertise as untested for LLMs. A cheap own test: real vs shuffled code recall, and top-down vs bottom-up debugging order.
